sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Albert J. Yano. Mr. Yano served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the 15th Air Force, 449th Bomb Group, 716th Bomb Squadron. He served in the European theatre and was based in Italy. His highest rank was tech sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Yano's home in Parma, Ohio, on July 29th, 2004. Albert was 80 at the time of this recording. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: And my army number was [redacted], which was an enlisted.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You'll never forget that, right?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Where was I at in 1941?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Living? Okay. I was living at 927 East 72nd Street, Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I was -- at that particular time I was 17.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Seventeen. Were you still in school?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have particular memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Absolutely. Absolutely. Yes. I remember exactly where I was at. I was in the front room of our apartment house on 72nd Street. I just remember that very clearly, you know, when that happened, but -- and when I went in, I volunteered for the service. I volunteered in 1942. It was about September or October. I'm not sure. I don't know if it says on the discharge or not. But, anyhow, I had just finished the tenth grade and I enlisted in the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You had to get your parents' signature probably.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yes, I did. Yes, I did. My mother signed for me. And I went into the Air Force. I guess they tested me for Morse Code when I first went in, you know, if I could, you know, remember duplicates and things like that. And so consequently I got into the Air Force. I went to Fresno, California, for my basic training, and then I went to Scott Field Illinois Radio School for I think three or four months I went there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day at training? What was that like?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Training. Yeah. It was -- it was unusual. It was different. I expected it, you know. I'll tell you a little incident that happened before that. I went from home to Camp Perry, and at Camp Perry we were there and a sergeant come in and says, I need a volunteer for KP. He says, Whoever volunteers now, he says, won't be on KP any more because that'll fulfill your duty. So I says, well -- he said, You got four hours to work, and he says most of the time KP could be 16, 18 hours. So I figured, well, I'll just volunteer and -- and cut my time down. So I volunteered, and the next morning we shipped out. So right then and there I learned you do not volunteer for anything in the service. That was the first day -- one of my first days in service, and I learned that you just don't volunteer for anything because, again, I got kind of taken. But then I went to Fresno, California. I think I spent -- it must have been a couple of months in basic training. I forget how long. Maybe it wasn't even that long. But anyhow then I went to Scott Field, Illinois, that's radio school. And also code, Morse Code we were going to learn there -- or we did learn there. And I went from -- from Scott Field to Laredo, Texas, for gunnery school. I went from Laredo, Texas -- I think I spent about maybe -- maybe a couple months there. And from Laredo, I went to Tucson, Arizona, where we started forming our crews, Davis-Monthan Air Force Base there in Tucson, Arizona, and we formed our base there. My name is Yano, Y-A-N-O, and when my crew members saw this posted on the board they thought I was a Jap. They thought I was a Japanese because Yano is a common Japanese name. But in Slovak actually it's pronounced "Jono," so that means John. But we formed a crew, practiced there. We did some practice runs on Chicago and St. Louis, night runs, bombing runs over those cities. Of course, they were just practice. Then we went to Topeka, Kansas -- no. Let's see. I went to Bruning. I went to Bruning and they started to -- Bruning, Nebraska, and they started to fade us in for going overseas, instructions, we got our clothes and everything that we needed for overseas. Then we went to Topeka, Kansas, where we actually got our planes to go overseas. We had our crews, had our practice missions, and we started overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with your crew?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Quite well. Yes. Very good, very good, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your position on the plane?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I was a radio operator, left gunner, left waist position. And we went from Topeka. Again, we were told about overseas. And we were going to go the southern route to Europe. So we flew into Trinidad and then down into South America. From South America, which is the shortest distance across the Atlantic, we went into Africa. We got into Africa. From Africa we went to -- let's see. We went from Africa right into our base at the instep -- the instep of Italy. In other words, Italy is a boot and right there at the instep is where our base was and it was a town -- the big town there was Bari, near there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: About when was that crossing?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: That was in '42. Yeah. That was in '42. That was in January -- February, January we did that.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: '42. '43 we started flying.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I thought you said you enlisted in '42.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I did. I enlisted in '42. Oh, that's right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So it would probably be early '43, right?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: It would be '43 when we -- let's see. Because '44 I was already captured.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: May 24th.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How many missions did you fly before you were captured?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I had 45 missions in.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So maybe you started flying in early '44, right? Is that right?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. We started flying our missions in early '44. That's right, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I'm trying to remember --

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: We flew over in '43. We flew over in '43, December, November and December of '43. Of course, we had some practice missions over there. And on our way over, we lost, I think, something like three planes that had hit a mountain and went down. I think one went in the ocean, and two of them hit a mountain over there which was an Air Force base. So they went in between two mountains and I guess they just didn't quite make it. In fact, the plane that crashed had mostly our officials in it. There were like 12 of the top brass of our group, and we lost them there. And we went from Africa into Italy and we started doing our missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first combat mission?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yes. It was Mostar in Yugoslavia. I remember that because when we went on this mission, of course, we were all green. Everybody was green. And we had B-24s that flew over us with the bomb bay doors open. And you don't want to be below a bomber when the bomb bay doors are open, you know. So I remember -- in fact, one of the planes did go down. One was damaged and one plane did go down and the bombs hit him, you know, they dropped right on him. So we come back --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were feeling on that first mission?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Very scared. Very scared. You know. Like I say, everybody says to us, well, we were kind of heroes, but we weren't heroes. We were a bunch of scared kids. We had a job to do and we did it, and that's the truth. And anybody can say that he wasn't scared when he was flying has got to be crazy because some of the missions that I had gone -- I mean I had gone into Budapest, which is the capital of Hungary, I went to Bucharest, which is the capital of Romania, I went to the capital of Yugoslavia which is Belgrade, and I hit Regensburg and the Ploesti oil fields. In fact, there was a German general on History Channel and the narrator asked him what would be one point that cost them the war in Europe, and he said, When we could not produce oil out of the Ploesti oil fields, he said, then we lost the war because we could not keep our equipment running, which is true. As everybody knows, they didn't have any gas and oil. So I think our group hit that -- the Ploesti oil fields 125 times. We'd just -- we'd go back every two or three days and just -- they would fix it, we'd bomb it, they'd fix it, we'd bomb it, and we'd burn it. So it got to be kind of a game, I guess, with us. In fact, the Tuskegee Airman were our cover, flying our cover. They flew the P-38s, the 47s -- P-47s and then of course P-51 came along. I flew all over Italy, Anzio. I had two missions at Anzio which was a beachhead near Rome and -- that our troops were kind of trapped on the beachhead. The Germans were in the mountains firing on them, and we would hit these mountains. Another thing is when we went on some of the missions up into northern Italy they would have us fly over the basilica where there was a big battle raging for quite a while there. And we just flew that -- we flew that way just to -- for the morale of the ground troops. They would stop and cheer; and when they'd see us, you know -- but there was quite a battle that had taken place there at the basilica. The Germans again were on high ground and our troops were trying to take it. I've gone on a number of missions where we -- where we would -- we would come back and the floor where we were at on the floor of the plane in the midsection where I was headed, the waist gun, the floor would be just covered with ammunition, shells, casings from the 50 caliber guns that we used to fight our way out of them. From '44 -- first part of '44 the Germans had quite a few fighters and high caliber 88 anti-aircraft guns which were very, very accurate. And a lot of missions used what they called window, and we would throw this out to try to deceive the radar. Radar would pick up this window and just be 50 miles away from there, 30 or 20 miles away, and they would be firing at this window, you know, because they -- they -- that's what the radar picked up.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was that like tinfoil?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: That is right. It's just like Christmas tinfoil, icicles -- icing that you put on a Christmas tree. That's exactly what it was. And we would drop boxes and boxes of this stuff, you know, throw it out the windows. And the name of it we called it at that time was windows. Let's see. I had gone to Balogna. That's the right pronunciation in Italy. I've gone to the Tower of Tolini (ph), Tower of Pisa, I've gone to Venice, marshaling yards all over Yugoslavia, Italy, most of the towns with transportation or shipping. We would usually go in and take out the railroad yards and the marshaling yards, which are the harbors.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you ever come close to hitting anything with your guns?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: With our guns, we hit 13 planes and three possibilities with our plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I'll tell you a little instance that had happened at the same target that I was shot down which is Viennois Chad, which is the German high command -- where the high command had living quarters and also they trained officers and also made airplane parts. I don't know if it was ball bearings or what they were, but they were making airplane parts there and it was a very highly protected target. And the name of it was Viennois Chad, and it's about 35, 40 miles south of Vienna. We had gone to this -- well, I'd gone there a couple times before, but this third mission, I think it was, when I went back there, we had -- we were just approaching the target. In fact, I think we were -- no, we weren't quite. We were just coming out of the target and the fighters were still on us. One of the -- I thought it was one but evidently it was two -- my right waist gunner said there was two planes -- had come into the place that I could hear the tail gunner not give up at all on his guns. By that I mean we were taught just to go boop, boop, boop, boop, and then stop and boop, boop, boop, boop and stop; and this guy here just laid on that gun and he just kept firing and firing. So, consequently, I did what I did. I was standing like this, standing straight up looking out, and I twisted this way here to look to the back of the plane and just that second that plane blew up. The plane blew up. And from what I understand the debris from that plane took down the second -- his wing man. Now, he blew up but the wing man just went down smoking, you know. So evidently he hit the proper -- he hit something to bring that man down. But anyhow one bullet had come into the plane. It had hit the tail gunner in the right boot. That did not cut the boot or anything. It just hit it in the boot, ricocheted off that boot, came and tore the flak jacket off my shoulder, 20 millimeter shell ripped the flak jacket off my shoulder, just the jacket, never drew blood or anything, knocked me down, and then went across the plane -- it ricocheted off me, went across the plane, hit a big oxygen bottle and ripped a hole about 18 inches in the top of our plane. So I know the Lord was with me then because had I been standing straight up like I was at first that thing would have hit me right in the neck. That bullet would have hit me right in the neck. See, I was this way and I went this way, like this here, see, and that's when that shell come in. And now you could just see the hole there. And right where it hit the ball gunner in the boot, come hit me in the shoulder, went across the plane and hit the oxygen bottle and ripped its way out. But he got one shot into it and evidently he was -- he was really on us, you know. I could see the face -- actually see the face of that pilot when that plane blew up. I mean everything happened just like that there. I saw the pilot, the plane blew up, and it knocked me down. Everything just happened in a split second. Of course, we had a number of experiences with fighters. We somehow somebody in our squadron evidently didn't care too much for us. We weren't what you could say a popular crew, and consequently we flew what's called tail end Charlie. We were always in the tail end position. And if you're in the tail end position, you do a lot of fighting with fighters. That's where they usually come in, at the tail end, although I had gone into Regensburg where they came in out of the sun and hit us from the front. But this time here -- we had many, many times that we had gotten into combat with fighters, you know, because they were still -- it was still -- in fact, I had seen that new jet fighter off in a distance, and they had -- they had a rocket that would burst white when it hit the air, you know, and we didn't know what they were, but we could see this plane. But at the time when I was flying that, the jet plane of the Germans could only stay in the air, we were told, for 13 minutes, so it wasn't really a problem for us, you know. But finally on this last mission that I did was -- we had taken off. We had got -- was going pretty good. We had what was known as -- we were the 449th Bomb Group and there was a group 450th which had painted their tails white, and they were called the Cottontails. So for some reason or other we had heard a story that one of their Cottontail planes was in trouble all by themselves, and German fighters pulled up -- a couple of German fighters pulled up to him. And the Cottontail, the B-24, dropped its wheels and signaled like he was going to land, and the planes came close to the plane and they shot them down. They shot both the German planes down and then got back to base. But I had read the book on the Cottontails, and they said that this is not true. But whatever it was that the Germans had they always hit these Cottontails; and we were, you know, in that wing with the Cottontails so consequently why we usually got a couple of stragglers that would be after us or they would be after us a number of times. But this particular day when we were going into Viennois Chad off to the right down below us we never -- all the squadrons and groups flew at different altitude so that the gunners could not get on us. If they hit a particular altitude, why then others would be out of that particular range. So this particular day off to the -- below us and off to the right of us was these Cottontails, and the Germans were all over these guys. The planes were all over them, just like bees attacking something. And B-24s were going down almost one right after another. I know I saw at least three B-24s go down, you know, and I don't know how many fighters they got; but the planes were going down, and they were really attacking them. Then we started our bomb run over the target, our IP. That's initial point, the point where we just keep a straight -- in other words the plane is on automatic pilot when they put it on that, the IP, and the plane just follows right to that particular point and that's the drop zone. So we had just -- we were on the IP, and the flak got pretty heavy and we dropped our bombs. And the last thing I heard on the interphone was, Bombs away. And then the next thing I heard was, Bomb bay doors close. Bam. That's when they hit us. They must have hit us twice, I figure, I think in the right wing because from what I understand the top gunner and the pilot -- co-pilot did not move once we were hit. In other words, I don't know if they were killed instantly. Of course, the intercom went out. So here we are in the back of the plane. We don't know what's going on outside of the fact that the plane is burning all over, you know. The right wing is burning, and pretty soon the left wing is burning and was shooting flames all the way back beyond the windows. And this other waist gunner and myself, we didn't know what to do. We thought maybe we'd -- it's been known that planes -- sometimes guys jump and the plane will go back, so it's kind of a tricky situation there. So we waited just a little bit too long, and the plane went into a spin. You get a B-24 in a spin, and there's nothing on God's earth that will straighten that sucker out again. Centrifugal force had him. He was trying to get out the waist window which he couldn't do because of the centrifugal force. I was pinned against the fuselage looking out at the ground at the escape patch right there or camera hatch or whatever they call it, you know. And I could see that. And I'm just right stuck against the fuselage because of the centrifugal force of the plane twisting. And I could see the ground turning. The ground was really turning, and I knew the ground wasn't turning, that we were in that spin. So I was kind of trapped there for a while, and this other waist gunner was, too. And all of a sudden that right ring where they had hit us came off. The wing came off. When that wing came off, the plane lurched to the right. That's when I went out, and he followed me right out. That's the only thing that saved us. If that wing stayed on, we would have never gotten out. I'd never have gotten out of that plane. The pilot, the co-pilot -- George Foote (ph) was the pilot. Madigan (ph) was -- Madigan -- Quentin P. Madigan (ph) was the co-pilot. George Foote (ph) was the pilot. And Lane (ph) and -- Gorel (ph) was the engineer, and Lane (ph) was the ball gunner. All four went down with the plane. The only thing, I didn't see the plane hit the ground, but I saw -- almost immediately saw the smoke and fire coming from where it hit the ground, you know. I wound up in a -- it's amazing how quiet it is when your chute opens up there. It's just very, very quiet, kind of a peaceful thing. I landed in some large -- well, what I did before I landed, I tried to steer the chute towards another chute that I had seen in the sky coming down. And when I did this, I almost dumped my chute. I figured I better not fool around with that thing because I didn't know that much about it and I figured I'd better just leave things the way they are because I sure didn't want to dump that chute, you know. By dumping it, I mean dump the air out of it and then it's just a trailing chute I'd be caught with. So I landed in some trees. They must have been a hundred, a hundred fifty feet high, those trees, I swear. They were pine trees. It wasn't a big forest, but it had quite a few of these pine trees and they were way up there. I landed in the pine tree. My chute landed up in there, and I swung over to the trunk, took off my chute, left it up -- of course left if up there -- it was stuck in the tree -- and started -- proceeded to go down. And in the process of going down the tree, about, I think, about maybe 15 foot from the ground my hands gave way and I did kind of a somersault in the air. Lucky I didn't land on my head. I probably still would have been there. But I landed on my feet. I went over to a bush and took off my Mae West and covered it up -- Mae West is the flotation device that we wear when we're flying -- and covered it up with some leaves. And then it was like a valley. I landed on one side and then ran across the valley over to the other side and hid in some bushes. I figured, well, I'll just sit here for a while and see if anything is going to happen. So it was about an hour later. Here come two guys through the woods. Both of them had clubs, and they're looking -- I know they're looking for fliers. Well, here I am sitting across the valley from them. They're on the side that I had come down. Evidently, they must have seen my chute and were looking for me on that side, but I had run across the valley and was on the other side. So they looked around for quite a while and they left. And I must have sat there for another quite a while. I had injured -- in the process of bailing out -- and I'm not sure exactly where this happened -- I had injured my -- injured my right ankle. I don't know where. Like I say, if it was in the tree, when I hit the tree, when I dropped out of the tree or someplace in that -- in the -- when the plane was in a spin, in the process of moving around the plane, someplace I had injured my ankle. And it was getting quite sore now. And I started walking. I walked for -- we hit that target probably around 9, 10:00 in the morning. And I think I started walking maybe about 11 or 12, something like that, and I walked for quite a while, walking in the shrubbery of the farms, you know, on the lines there. It had all the shrubberies. And trying to keep myself hidden as best as I could. And here I had an escape package. In that package I had one map. I think it was of Yugoslavia. There was no money in the package, which there should have been. There should have been three compasses in the package. I only had one compass, which was about the size of my thumbnail. So I started walking south. But the more I held the compass in my hand the more it steamed up. I couldn't read it, you know. So I just tried to walk what I thought was south anyhow. Of course, getting back would have been quite an operation because I had been across the Alps. This was Diane (ph). So I would have had to cross the Alps probably between seven and eight hundred miles from our base. So I knew that I would probably need help, by that maybe get into the underground or something like that if I could. So I walked for about -- probably about five or six hours, and finally my ankle had really gotten big. It was all swollen up. And so I says, well, I either got to get help or I gotta -- I can't go any farther. So I walked up to this farmhouse, which I should have gone probably into the barn and just sit in the barn because there was a Polish girl there. She was a forced labor, you know, Polish girl, and she may have been able to help me. But this farmer came out with a double barrel shotgun, and I knew he wasn't going to help me. And some people picked me up and they took me to a burgermeister of a little town. I don't remember -- I don't know what the name of that little town was. They took me to this little town and they talked and talked and they asked me questions, and I just gave them my name, rank, and serial number. And they searched me, and they took me to a hospital because they could see my ankle was badly swollen, you know. I could barely -- I just couldn't hardly walk with it any more, you know. So they took me to this hospital, I think in Viennois Chad. That's where they were bombed.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Is that near Vienna? Is that what you said?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. It's about -- Viennois Chad is about, I'd say, between 30 and 40 miles almost directly south of Vienna. And they took me to this hospital, and the doctor looked at it and bandaged it up that night. And when I woke up in the morning I -- they had me in the hall because they had so many people there. They had me in the hall, and I heard someone talking and I recognized the voice of our bombardier. And his name was Murphy. I says, Hey, Murph. And he heard me. He says, Who is that? I said, Yano. And he says, My goodness. He says, What are you doing here? I says, Well, I'm -- I says, I'm in here. My leg is -- there's something wrong with my ankle. So I went in to see him, hobbled in there, and there he was with three or four other guys that they had been in their beds, you know, and I think he had broken some ribs. I'm not sure exactly what it was, but I know he broke a couple of ribs when his chute opened. If you're not in the right position -- and I don't know that much about a parachute jump -- but I know that if you're not in the right position if you're going forward and that thing snaps you back it'll break some ribs for you. So there he was with his broken ribs. So we talked for a while. And they moved me out of there that morning. They sent me to a barracks that they had been collecting all these fliers from the 440 -- 450th and 449th. All the planes had gone down they were collecting. The fliers just kept coming in, I mean. And I met most of my crew there. They had all been caught. From there on, they waited a couple days until they had what they figured had bailed out or been in the area, and they moved us. We went through Vienna, caught a train, had gone over to Frankfurt, Germany, Frankfurt, Germany. I think that one is the one that's on the Main, Frankfurt on the Main I think it is. It's on the eastern -- western part of Germany. I'm pretty sure that that's what that is. And we went through there. And we went through a -- we went through the railroad station there. And they have a large, large canopy over their railroad station that it's all glass. Of course, there wasn't one glass standing in it. They were all gone. And the metal was pretty well twisted up, too. So we we're going through there. And I remember an old man with a cane. He tried to -- he tried to hit me with the cane, but the guard stopped him. The guard stopped him, you know, kept him away from me. Now I had heard when we were going through this station that they had hung either three or four American fliers or three or four British fliers in the station there, the people had. So the Americans and British hit that Frankfurt, I think, three or four days in a row. And they let them know that if they hang any more fliers in there that they would completely destroy the city. I don't know how badly it was destroyed anyhow, but they said that they would completely destroy the city. So I guess that cut down the hanging -- cut the hangings down. But then we went into -- I think it was Dulog (ph). They called it Dulog (ph). We went to Dulog (ph), and we went into solitary confinement. They put us in solitary confinement. I was in there for, I think, two days in solitary confinement, and they would interview us. And, of course, being a radio operator I had the rank of tech sergeant. There wasn't much I could tell them outside of my name, rank, and serial number. But they kept me there for two days, very small room, window way up high, bed -- I don't know exactly how wide it was but it wasn't very wide, just enough room in there for a bed, a single bed. And from there, from Dulog (ph), we went to -- I think the camp was called Wetzlar where they gave us American clothes. They gave us clothes, GI clothes, heavy -- heavy coat, heavy coat and shoes, and stuff like that because most of us were just wearing flying clothes. By that, I mean we had electric suits on and we had, you know, just flying clothes on. So they gave us these GI issued clothes and sent us into Stetten, up there by Stetten, up there by the North Sea -- or is that the Baltic Sea up there I believe, way up north there? Northeast Germany would be the Baltic Sea up in Stetten, where Stetten is at. And they had built a new camp up there. This new camp, I think we were one of the first people to come into this camp. This new camp was built with all the mistakes that they had made at Stalag Louvre III where the British fliers had all escaped under tunnel and escaped from that camp. By that I mean they had built these barracks on stilts. They built them where they were about four foot off the ground. And at night they had the German dogs in there and the guards roaming around. So there was no way of digging out of this camp. This camp, I think, was almost foolproof as far as anybody escaping, you know. I don't think I've ever heard of anybody escaping from this Stalag Louvre IV. And I was there for, oh, probably, let's see, May, June. I got there in June and probably I was there until, I think, the first part of '45. That would be '45, yeah, because we shipped out of there in boxcars. They loaded us all in these little boxcars of theirs, cattle cars, and they would just barely all of us could sit down at one time. They really packed us in there. And anybody with claustrophobia would be in really bad shape, you know, which I had a case of it, you know. I felt like I was, you know, just so close that, you know, I got just a slight case of this claustrophobia. But anyhow this particular boxcar we were in must have been a refrigeration car because it was very, very tightly sealed. By that I mean we could barely get any air in there because I remember sitting there in January in my shorts in this boxcar because it was so hot in there, and I took cans of -- we had K rashes and the cans would be cold. I'd rub them on my face, you know, to try to cool myself down. Of course, some of it was probably nerves. We were pretty well packed in this car. And about the second day out one of the fellas died in there. He -- a fella got up in the morning and said, Jesus, get off of me already. He said, God damn it, you've been laying on me all night. So he gave him a shot, and he went over to the next guy. He laid on the fella to the next guy, and the guy says, Well, don't lay on me, you know, and they felt him and he was already cold, you know. So they banged on the door and they took him out of there. I don't know. He was a little bit on the heavy side and he was quite a big guy. And I don't know what the circumstances were or why he died, but they took him away. And they had these carts with big wheels that they used to use to move baggage with, you know, the real large wheels at the station. They would have these big carts. And they would pick up bodies, maybe six or eight bodies almost every day from the train, you know, where the fellas had died. And finally after about -- well, we were -- we were -- we were moving from Stetten and they were talking us to Nuremberg, a camp at Nuremberg. So the Russians were coming so we had to get out of that Stalag Louvre IV. So they moved us. In the process of moving us, we went through Berlin. And during the time we were in Berlin the British had pulled an air raid on Berlin, and they -- of course, they took off. All the guards took off for bomb shelters and left all of us in the boxcars during this raid. So that was kind of a little -- in fact, it was very scary sitting there and bombs going off around you. And finally they didn't hit us and we got into Nuremberg. Well, they took us into a camp. The Italians were in there prior to us. And it was a very, very dirty, just-about-falling-apart place. The food was terrible. There were maggots in the soup. Of course, most of the soup contained dehydrated cabbage and a lot of rotten tomatoes -- potatoes rather. And to bring up a point, my friend at Stalag Louvre IV had found the bone of a dog jaw in his soup, you know, and of course they probably -- anything they could find they would throw it into the soup where it looked like meat. There was usually -- sometimes there was red meat in it which was horse meat. If any of them died, why they probably cut them up and throw them in there. But anyhow the food there at Nuremberg was very, very bad. It was, like I say, there were maggots in it. The only thing I did was move into a dark corner where I couldn't see them, and I still ate the soup which is -- some people tell me there's protein in maggots. I mean they were dead. They were not alive. They were dead. They boiled the soup and killed them. The British hit this Nuremberg. They were, I think looking for _____. But the word was _____+ ammunition dump. And they had dropped these red flares, and the Germans with their big lights were trying to find them in the sky. In fact, the Germans did get one of the planes, a British Lancaster or whatever they were they were flying, and dug fox holes and got into them, you know. _____+ just dumb enough to _____+ barracks, you know. I don't know if I'd have dug a hole anyhow; but, anyhow, I stood there and watched them. And it was -- it was -- it was really something. It would have made a really good movie with these flares coming down like that and the Germans shooting like crazy with their spotlights up there and the bombs hitting. And I think they finally did hit something because there was a big explosion. I don't know if they hit this ammunition dump or whatever. But my friend that was -- that was my right waist gunner, his name was Walter Gaits (ph). And he was my waist gunner. I'm going to have to go back and describe a little incident that happened in Stalag Louvre IV when we were going through it. But he said that those bombs at Nuremberg had moved the barracks off the foundation, you know. That's how hard the concussion was. And I'm going to go back to this little story back to Stalag Louvre IV when we were first going into this camp. Walter Gaits (ph) and myself and a fella by the name of Skidmore (ph), which was our tail gunner, and another one was Salior (ph), his last name was Salior. He was the nose gunner. And Walter said it was his compass and I said it was my compass; but, anyhow, it was that compass that was about the size of a fingernail, the right -- your thumbnail. We had gotten a _____ and we gently took it all apart and broke it down in the middle and cut out the middle and put this compass, this small compass into this hole. And we put everything back together, wet it as best we could, wet it and put it all back together. And when we were coming into -- now, Walter was right ahead of me when we were coming into this camp. And there was a big fella there. They called him Big Stoop. He was a German guard, and he was kind of rough on the soldiers, on the American soldiers. I mean every once in a while he'd slap one of them or kick them or whatever; and he was, you know, was quite hard on the American soldiers. He was the only one that I remember of ever touching the soldiers. So this big moose -- Big --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Stoop.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Stoop, Stoop, yeah, Big Stoop, took this bar of soap and he went like this here against the table, broke that thing open, saw that compass, and tried to say that the American Red Cross had put it in there, you know. And Walter was No, no, no, no. He says, We put it in there. So they put him in solitary confinement, I think, for about a week. So consequently he was not in the same barracks with me because he got -- he come out five days later and went into a new group of people. But this Big Stoop, like I say, he was kind of hard on the American soldiers. When we were liberated, I finally ended up in Moosburg, yeah, Moosburg, yeah, in Moosburg. When we were liberated in Moosburg by Patton and his army, we -- I guess some of the guys got together and they cut his head off. I saw him on the side of a road where they had taken his head off, you know, because a lot of guys were hit by him. And he was -- he was very mean. So I guess maybe a bunch of them got together and overpowered him and they took his head off. But getting back to Nuremberg now, we're at Nuremberg probably, oh, I don't think we were there more than a couple of weeks, if I remember right, maybe a month. I really don't remember. But we left Nuremberg on a march. We were marching from Nuremberg to Moosburg. They kept moving us because they wanted to keep us in front of the Russians. Incidentally, Hitler had issued an order to kill all American and British fliers because of what we had done to his country, you know. His buildings were in terrible shape, terrible shape. I mean they hit the cities. You know, Hitler started hitting London and we reciprocated by hitting his cities. So Germany was in bad shape. It was in ruins. And he had issued the order to kill all American and British fliers. But the German guards would not carry out the order because they knew by then that the war was over. The war for them was over, you know. It was just a matter of time and it would be over with. So they never did carry out his orders. But they just kept moving us. And we moved from Nuremberg to Moosburg over a two-week period marching on -- most of the time I think we were on the Audubon, big brand new highway. We slept in fields and barns and wherever, you know, and we finally got to Moosburg. And that camp was in very, very bad shape. But we got to Moosburg and we were in Moosburg probably maybe a month or month-and-a-half, and -- END OF FIRST CD SECOND CD BEGINS Well, what happened Patton's army liberated us there at Moosburg. He came through there. I saw Patton come through with his fancy side guns, and there was a half track in front of him and a jeep with a 50 caliber mounted, and he was in like a weapon -- not a weapon's carrier but a personnel carrier. And then there was another jeep with a 50 caliber and another half track was behind him, you know, and he'd come buzzing through that town, this little town of Moosburg. I think it was a couple days after the troops had gone through. They had blew a bridge. There was a river there, and the Germans blew the bridge. But the American engineers, they had that replaced in about a day and tanks were already on the move. Thomas A. Swope:: Did he _____ the prisoners at all when he got there?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. He just went right through. He went right through, no. He just went flying through that town. I mean his tanks did, too. I mean the town -- it was a small town and it had small roads, and them tanks going through the town just took off buildings. They would just, you know, go around a corner. They'd take the whole side of the building off, you know. And -- so some fellas had gone into town and they had got food from the American soldiers such as K rations and C rations and stuff like that, you know. So I figured, well, I'm going to go into town and I'm going to get myself something. Nobody was willing to go with me, so I went alone. So I went to this -- I went to town -- I met one of his lieutenants. I don't know what he was at the particular time that lieutenant -- yes, he was, he was making himself a hot meal. You know, he was heating something up. And I got to talking to him. And he said this is the first time in a month that he had a hot meal, that this crazy Patton, they called him blood and guts, and everybody called him our blood and his guts, he said that he just keeps going and going and going. He said they don't have time to make a hot meal. He said, The only time he stops is if he runs out of gas. And this was true. He would run out of gas and then of course he'd have to stop until the gas supplies came up and ammunition and whatever, you know, supplies came up. But this guy says, I haven't eaten a hot meal in a month. So I figured, well, I did get food from some of the tanks going through town, you know. I told him I was a prisoner of war, American, and they'd throw me some K rations and C rations. And somehow -- and I really don't remember how -- I got into this one German house. I'd gone into this German house. I may have gone there to ask for bread. That's probably what I did because I would go up to some houses and ask them for bread, you know. And these people invited me in and had given me a meal. They gave me coffee and some other things. I don't remember just exactly what they were. And on the wall hanging there was a soldier with an iron cross on his -- on the picture. He had -- the actual iron cross was right there, and I asked them who that was. I think they said it was their son or something, his son there or her son rather or else her husband. I don't remember. And I wanted that iron cross so bad. I figured I'm gonna take that iron cross. I could not make myself take that iron cross off that picture. I mean these people were so nice to me. I could not make myself take that iron cross. So consequently I didn't get that iron cross. But I got back into camp, and one of the fellas -- one of my friends come over and says, Hey, Yano, he says, you better go see -- the captain wants to see you. He says, They had a roll call and you're AWOL, you know. I said, Oh shit, here we go. So I went over. Then I saw the captain and he's telling me -- he says, I'm going to have you court martialed and all this kind of bullshit. I'm thinking to myself, You son of a bitch, you just come over here. I mean I don't know about swearing on these things, but anyhow --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's fine. That's fine.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: You know, I says -- you know, I mean he's coming over here and he's going to court martial me after what I had gone through? And finally he said, Well, he said, I'm not going to court martial you, he said, but you're going to be the last one to leave -- you're going to be one of the last ones to leave this camp. And all the screw-ups were the last ones to leave the camp, you know. We had -- everybody was gone and we had all the blankets and pots. And one fella had gone into town and got a cow. And we butchered that cow; and we, you know, had steaks and whatever, you know. But one guy -- I controlled my eating, you know, because I knew that I couldn't eat too much. And one guy ate too much and he died. He died from overeating because his stomach just couldn't take it. So we were the last ones to leave. We were the last C-47 who left there -- or DC-3. I think they were both the same plane. DC-3 and C-47, I think, were both the same plane. But we left there and we went to Camp Lucky Strike on the French coast. They had this camp. One of them was Lucky Strike. I guess they had Chester Field. But anyhow I landed in Camp Lucky Strike, and they gave us new clothes and they deloused us and cut our hair and, you know, they just really took care of us and gave us good food. And we were at the camp one day and Eisenhower came in. And he talked to the troops for a while, all PWs. And he was telling me -- he asked -- he says, What can we -- what can I do for you to make things better here, easier for you? And one of the GIs popped up and he said, We'd like to get something between the noon meal and the evening meal, you know, like a snack in between. So he ordered us eggnog. They'd give us eggnog about two, three o'clock in the afternoon, I forget what time it was, but they would give us eggnog; and that was pretty nice. There was one fella there who was in the barracks, and he had hung himself in the barracks. Now, this is the story that I had heard. His father had told him, If you ever get captured, he said, don't you ever come home. He said, You're a prisoner, he says, because you fight until you die, you know. And so consequently this fella, I guess, didn't want to go home. But anyhow that's the story I heard. Whether it was true or not, I really don't know. Now, I got a little story. Can you turn that off? (Tape recorder was shut off.)

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's part of it.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Okay. All right. I mean are you on tape now?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. We're rolling now.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: What happened at Camp Lucky Strike is -- did I say about the guy that hung himself?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: We got that part.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I told this friend of mine that I was going to go to Paris and I had to get a piece of tail. And he told me, he says, no, he wouldn't go with me because he was afraid he would get court martialed and then wouldn't get home on time or something, you know, that they would keep him there. So I says, Well, okay. I says, I'm gonna go to Paris. And I says, I'm gonna get laid and when I get laid I'll be back and if they're waiting for me to court martial me they can do whatever they damn well please, I says, but I'm gonna go to Paris and get laid. I had no idea how to go to Paris anyhow. I mean I just figured I'd get into a busy town and then find out which road went to Paris and hitchhike, you know, American soldiers were moving around in. So I got out on the road and I'm walking. Where these two black guys came from -- they were American soldiers. Evidently there was a camp -- Well, there was Camp Lucky Strike and Camp Chester Field and, you know, Marlboro. It might have been in that same area. So they probably worked at one of the bases. And I had -- I had a feeling that these black fellas -- two black guys were maybe going to rob me. But we went for a while. Maybe I had just misjudged them, I don't know, but I just had that feeling. But they left. They had turned off the road, and they told me that if I go this way here I would get into this little town and maybe I could make some connections there to get a ride to Paris. I'm still walking down the road here and pretty soon there's two girls. Where they came from I'll never know, but there was two girls on the road just ahead of me. So I walked up to these girls. In fact I hollered to them, I think, and I had befriended them and we walked for a while. And somehow, you know, it doesn't -- it doesn't take a -- you don't have to be able to talk everybody's language to talk about sex. So I asked -- I asked one of these girls if she would go up on the hill with me there, you know. So she went up on the hill and I had sex. And I come back down. And I paid her in American money which they had given us. And I went back to camp. When I went back to camp, this friend of mine says -- I told him the story. He says no. He says I was lying. He says, There's no way, he says, you could have got it that soon. He said, You've only been gone three or four hours. I told him, I says, Well, look, I went to the nurse, the nurse or whatever it was there, the Red Cross -- not the Red Cross but it was the emergency room, and I got a bottle of this -- I had gotten a prophylactic -- a prophylactic kit. And in this kit is a bottle with -- like it's a bottle you squeeze and you empty this fluid from the bottle up into your penis for venereal disease or any kind of disease. But I got this bottle and I was squeezing it, you know, and putting it in my penis. And this fella said to me -- he says, Yeah, he says, you must have got laid. He said, You would never be doing that, he said, if you hadn't got laid. So I -- I was pretty happy then, and then we shipped off. We shipped off for -- well, I don't know if I told that one about Eisenhower coming in?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. We got that.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: You got that one. Yeah. So then we went on a troop train -- not a troop train but a troop ship out of Camp Lucky Strike there in France. And in the process I had invested $300 into a crap game, which I lost. That was the amount that I was gonna lose, you know, and I really believe that one fella there, he probably had loaded dice or whatever you want to call them or something because he just had bundles of money in his hand. He had just taken everybody. I didn't know that -- I never knew that much about what you could do with dice or anything but, anyhow, he had really -- I bet he had 10, 15 thousand dollars in his hand -- in his pockets and hands. So I arrived at New York, and I can't think of that camp that we went to up there. I don't know what the name of that camp is.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Possibly Camp Kilmer (ph)?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Kilmer (ph) was in New Jersey I think.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. It wasn't Kilmer (ph). I don't know what camp it was. But anyhow we went into a camp there and they processed us. And I had had this sword with me and I had some other --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you mention where you got that German sword?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I'll be truthful. Well, they had these Germans -- they had these Germans, the soldiers and officers, in a barn. And evidently I must have gotten it in this barn from these soldiers, you know, because to be truthful with you I really don't remember where I got that thing, you know. But I remember being in this barn. They were -- American soldiers were guarding it. And in there they had all these German soldiers. So evidently I must have got it there. So I had this sword with me and some other things that I had brought back from Germany because they said no use in taking anything home because they're going to take it away from you. Well, they didn't take it away from me. Then I got a train -- no. Let's see. No. I was supposed to go by train. In fact, I had called home and told them I'm coming by train, but something happened that -- something was delayed. So what I did is I walked over to the Greyhound. I took a Greyhound bus and I come home. And I don't know if you remember Greyhound used to be on Ninth Street and downtown, you know. They used to have a bus station there. And, of course, you come in by train at the terminal tower. So I come in by bus from New York and I got off at the bus station there at Ninth Street and Superior, right close to Ninth and Superior. What I did is I walked down to the terminal tower because I'd called home and they said -- well, my sister and my girlfriend had been waiting for me at the terminal tower because they thought I was coming in by train, which I told them I was coming in by train, but everything changed then. I went down there and there they are waiting and I'm walking in from the outside in there, and so we met there. That's just about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what was that reunion like?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yes. It was quite a reunion. You know, I'll tell you. When I came across that main avenue bridge there and I saw the terminal tower, I just -- I dropped a few tears because I said, I'm home. When I saw that terminal tower coming across that bridge I says, I'm home. That really hit me then, you know. So it was quite a reunion. My girlfriend and I we were -- let's see. About April 29th I think I was liberated. By the time I got home -- we got married I think in August -- no, July. We got married in July. And then I was going to go back. They had me come back for going back to Miami Beach. We were going to go to Miami Beach and were going to stay there for a while and they were going to retrain us on B-29s. And while I was home in August -- I had a three-month leave. All POWs got three-month leaves. I had a three-month leave. In the meantime, I had gotten married. So just before I had left in August to go back to Florida, why the war had ended in Japan. They had dropped those bombs. So we went down there and they debriefed us, and it was pretty nice down there. We really had it nice, you know. The wife was there and we really -- and all my friends were there. So we had it pretty nice. But they shipped me to Camp Atterbury right away because I had -- see, everything was on a point system and I mean I had points I mean like two or three times more than most people did, you know. So I got to Camp Atterbury in Indiana, and they got me out of there in a hurry. And of course I had had enough in the army. I said, That's it. I want to get out. I don't care. I didn't go for teeth or I didn't go for -- I should have really got a bump up. I was a -- see, I was a tech sergeant, two stripes below, you know, and I should have got a master sergeant because if you're a prisoner of war you get a bump up on rank, which my right gunner did. He was a staff sergeant. He went to tech sergeant. I should have went to master sergeant. But I didn't want to dillydally with anybody. I just wanted out. That's all there is to it. I had had enough. By then I really had enough of it, so I told them, I says, No, I want out. I mean I didn't know anything about the bump up on rank; otherwise I would have taken it, you know, if it would have meant a couple days or something like that. I just wanted to get out of Camp Atterbury. I had married and the wife was there. So I wanted to go home. That was enough. The war was over and that's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How did you get your Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Well, that's what I said. I don't know exactly where it happened. I had injured my right foot. That's where I got the Purple Heart. Because they had German records that I was in the hospital. That's how I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's how you got the Purple Heart.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: My dad was awarded a Purple Heart after he was captured, and I've never been able to find out how --

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Especially if he was in the hospital. They probably -- they had the German records on me. Let me grab that. Yeah. That -- that's what I got it for. I'll tell you the truth, I think there was something broken in that because I limped for a couple, three months, four months after that, you know, when I was in camp. But I don't know what. They said -- evidently, they thought I was okay so they let me go. Of course, there's -- they were pretty good there at the hospital, the German doctors. They were really good. I mean they took care of me and fed me and cleaned me up. So I can't complain about my treatment there in Germany. The only thing is that I have anything to complain about is the food. The food was terrible, you know. Nobody ever abused us. As long as you -- and we were told that there's -- there's a lot more safety in numbers, you know what I mean? If they catch you -- like my friend, Walter Gaits (ph), the right gunner, he had escaped and he was loose for about two months. But I was -- they kept telling us, stay together, stay together. If we stay together, your chances of making it are pretty good. In fact, he had run into a German officer that he felt was gonna shoot him, you know, but there was two young German soldiers there. And he said -- he said that's why he thinks he didn't shoot him because he had found them in the woods there with these -- with another guy, I guess. They were in the woods hiding, you know, and these two German soldiers had found them. And then this officer -- they were shooting at a tree or something, and this officer come back to see what was going on. And he said that he really thought this officer wanted to shoot him, you know, but he said because of these two German soldiers, he said, he didn't do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How many guys got out of your plane? Six?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Six. Four went down with the plane. The pilot, the co-pilot, the top gunner, and the belly gunner all went down with the plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were all six captured?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Uh-hum. Uh-hum. Yeah. We outlived -- we -- we all came home, you know. None of us died over there, I mean outside of the ones that had bailed out. We all came home. This one friend of mine, Walter, he's still alive. He's 84 years old. He's in the Florida Keys. He has a home down there. I think he's in the process of selling it. We bought a boat together down there. He's on a canal, so we bought a boat together there about 15 years ago and we'd fish down there when he was fishing. He won't fish any more. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you were flying, did you have a good luck charm of any sort?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. Prayer. Prayer. Prayer was my good luck. He was with me all the time, all the time. And I'll tell you -- when we were over there in Italy -- see, this camp -- I mean this air field that we had gone into, the Americans had bombed, you know. I mean it had craters all over the place. Then of course they'd fill up these craters and use them for themselves. I mean it was raining over there. During the wintertime we were flying starting in January. There would be rain and a little bit of snow, not much snow in southern Italy, you know. You don't get too much snow. But anyhow they would fill up with water. I mean as we would be taking off, the plane would go joom, joom, and loaded with ten 500-pound bombs, full load of gasoline, and trying to get this sucker off the what'd-you-call. And these runways weren't that long, you know. And then it's hitting these chuckholes. Boom, boom. Water goes on spraying into the plane. And I would just be sitting there praying that we got this sucker off the ground. I'll tell you, it did -- and this is when we first got there. After a while they fixed the place. I mean they may have even black-topped it, I don't know. But when we first started flying, that base was in terrible shape. We were in -- in a German -- it was probably an officers' quarters or something, buildings all made out of marble, and we were living in there. At first, we were sleeping on the floors. We had a room for the enlisted man. The officers had their own place. These were just enlisted men in this building, you know, six crews, crew members from each crew. There would be six over here and six over here and so on. And we heated those places -- we had make-shift heaters that we made. We would use a hundred octane fuel, which is no fuel to use for trying to keep warm with, and they would take copper tubing we'd get from mechanics and we'd drop it down in there. And then we would put it on -- if you could find a fire brick or something like that, you'd put it on that fire brick and burn it, you know. Well, that worked good as long as it was working. But one night right across from us we were -- there's a big hallway. We were over here in this room, and there's another room over here had this crew over here. And one of these assholes came in the night. He may even have been drunk, you know, and he's going to put more hundred octane gasoline in the storage tanks that drifts down into this -- stones or stones or whatever we could find to burn it in, you know, a fire brick. Consequently, he spilled the God damn thing, and boy, oh boy, talk about a fire. That hundred octane with these guys sleeping in there and we're right across the God damn hall, you know, and, man, it was an inferno in there. I opened the door and I told him, I said, (?Shiff,?) we may have to go out the window, you know. I said, Boy, that place is really burning. I saw one guy running down the hallway and the fumes must have been there and then all of a sudden that fire went down right after him, you know. This fella, Gaits, (ph) he got his ears burned, you know. He tried to pull fellas out of that room. And it was a real mess. Quite a few of them got burned up pretty bad. I mean nobody was killed. Nobody died. But they were -- some of them had some really bad burns. Incidentally, there was one crew. See, I used to fly with different crews because I was a radio operator and a lot of crews didn't have radio operators. So consequently I would pinch hit for these other crews. Well, there was one crew. This was his name. The pilot's name -- you always went by the pilot's name. So his name was Roberts. So that was the Roberts crew. I had flown with him for maybe three or four times, and he finally asked me. He says, Yano, why don't you join our crew? He says, I'd like you to be our radio operator. And I told him -- I said, No. I says -- I said, I got my crew and, you know, it's just like family. I said, No, I can't leave my crew. So we were friends. And he was the type of guy we would be coming back off formation and he would leave the formation and he'd go down and strafe God damn trains down on the ground. You know, a B-24 wasn't made to strafe planes on the ground. So he was kind of -- he was known for his craziness, you know. And then I found out after the war was over that his plane had blew up and killed all ten of them. All of them were killed. So I was kind of glad I didn't join his crew. But he was a real wild man.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you like the B-24?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. I liked it. You know, I mean the only thing that -- I think it blew up fast, you know. I mean sometimes you would -- there would be nobody get out. The plane would blow up and nobody would get out of it, you know. But -- yeah. Well, you know, the B-24 -- I know they give the B-17 a lot of credit, but we could do everything better than the 17. We could go higher, we could carry a bigger bomb load, we could go further. We could do everything the B-17 couldn't do. And did you know -- I don't know whether you knew this or not -- the B-17, there was 12,000 of them built. The B-24 there was 18,000. That B-24 was the most planes of any plane in the world that -- that were built that, you know, there was 18,000 B-24s built. See, they wanted them for the South Pacific, and then of course the 29 came in, you know. But, yeah, they were using them pretty heavy in the South Pacific. We could do everything better than the B-17. But, you know, one of the reasons the 17 got so much credit for everything is because, see, we were -- most of the 24s were in Italy, most of the 17s were in England, and everybody wanted to go to England to stay, you know. The reporters and all the announcers and all that kind of stuff would go to England because the living there was a hell of a lot better than Italy, so everybody went there. Consequently, the B-17 was big there, and that's why they lavished all this fame and everything on the B-17. But the B-17 was not the plane that the B-24 was, I'll tell you that. But everybody -- everybody was in England and of course the 8th Air Force was loaded with all the officers. They were the first ones there, you know. So they grabbed all the glory and the B-17 grabbed all the -- the flying fortress was the big, you know, big, big thing. Well, they couldn't do hardly anything that we could do, you know. We could do everything. We could go faster, higher, farther, have a bigger bomb load, and everything. I think they could only carry eight 500-pounders. We carried ten.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You were with the 15th Air Force.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. 15th Air Force, yeah, 449th Bomb Group, and 716th Bomb Squadron. Yeah. It was -- I'll tell you what, I was 19 years old when I was a prisoner of war.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you say you flew 45 missions?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Forty-five missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you flew with a variety of crews?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. I flew most of them with my crew.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did that plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: We had -- we had a lot -- we had a number of planes. We went on leave one time and our plane -- we had one called -- the one I went down with was the Shamrock. Our pilot and co-pilot and our navigator and bombardier I think they were all Irish. So it was called the Shamrock. But Shackwolf (ph). That's it. We had a plane called Shackwolf (ph). We had gone to Regensburg in Germany which was really, really a bad mission. We fought like crazy over there with fighters. We had gone to R and R, you know, rest and recuperation, and another crew took our plane. It was shot down. We went to Regensburg the first raid there to Regensburg and we come back and we went to R and R. Well, this crew picked up our plane, and they flew it and they went down. It was shot down on the second mission to Regensburg which was a really, really bad target. That's where I told you the planes had come in from the -- they come in from the sun, from the front. Mostly they came in from the back end of it, but this time here they came out of the sun right down the front of us. I mean when they came down there was a formation, I would say, of probably at least 40, 50 planes coming in at one time. And, you know, being shot down in -- in the Alp -- in the Alps, you know, you might as well shoot yourself if you got a gun with you. You might as well cut your throat or do something because there's no way in hell you're gonna get out of them Alps, you know, I mean to parachute down into those Alps there. And you might be miles. You have no idea which way to start even walking. And the snow could be ten foot deep up there, you know. So I -- that was -- that was a bad deal. That was a bad deal. And we flew over the Alps a lot. We hit -- what else did we hit up there? We hit another little town up there, another someplace up in there. Well, we hit Venice. Like I said, we hit Anzio. I hit Anzio twice. That was the beachhead. I got a whole list of towns that I had hit, you know, in northern Italy and also in Yugoslavia. There was one fella had gone on a mission and he was a friend of mine and he didn't have any heated boots. So he borrowed my boots, my heated electric boots, you know. We had electricity boots. A lot of times I didn't wear them clothes because after you'd bend in them so much the God damn things would like catch on fire in these places here where you bend them a lot, you know. The damn things would short circuit. So I had lent him my flying boots. And he was shot down. And about three months later he came through -- the Partisans, I think, brought him back through and he got -- they got him back to the base and he had them shoes. He said, Van, he said, I wore them suckers out. They were. They were worn out, you know. But, yeah, we had some fellas that were shot down and then they would get in with the Partisans and stay and do the fighting with them and the whole bit and then they would -- they'd bring them back and ship them back over to Italy. We had one woman in there one time. She had come into camp. I had seen her. She wasn't in any of the buildings but anyhow I had seen her. And they said that they had to get her out of Yugoslavia. They said she had choked something like six or eight German officers, you know. You know, she was really a beauty but evidently she was a spy. They said that she had -- and they knew -- they had found out that she had killed some officers -- German officers. So they got her out of Yugoslavia. Oh, yeah, one other thing. There used to be a fella that sold almonds, you know, peanuts. He'd come around and sell peanuts, you know, and we'd buy peanuts from him. I found out later when I was in the prison camp that he was a German spy, that he'd come around and get information and see everything that was going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Wow. Any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: No. Well, there's a bunch of them. I mean those are the big ones. You know, I had gone to -- these fliers that we had, these black guys, you go across the Adriatic -- is that the Adriatic? Yeah, the Adriatic. There's Yugoslavia. Here's the Danube River. So what they would do they would fly from our base over to the Danube River. Heck, they didn't have enough gasoline. So we would go from here over to either Bucharest -- there's another town called Brezov. I hit there in Yugoslavia, too. We had hit Bucharest or Ploesti oil fields here. And what would happen, these German fighters would knock the hell out of us over here coming, you know, all the way to the target. And the German fighters would be on us, you know, because we had no fighter cover. Then we get over to the target and the anti-aircraft fire would start, you know. So we would have -- you know, we'd be shot to hell by anti-aircraft fire. We'd leave that. Back again the Germans would pick us up again. By the time these escorts come back to pick us up, it was all over with. So these black guys are telling -- I guess they made a movie -- where they never lost a bomber. Well, that is bullshit. That is so much bullshit, you know. I would like to get one of these Tuskegee. I mean we went -- we went overseas in our squadron. This is the 716th -- 716th Bomb Squadron. We went overseas with 180 men. Of that 180 men, 18 men came home. The rest were either killed or prisoners of war.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So I guess what they're leaving out is that they meant while they were escorting the bombers they didn't lose one.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Well, evidently, that's what they're talking about, but I mean I would have to bring it up to them that, Look, you guys kill. So what good -- you were no good to us at all. I says, you might as well have stayed home as far as going with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: There was nobody attacking while they were escorting.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: That's right. That's exactly right. As soon as they hit the Danube River, they'd turn around and go back, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Then the P-51 came. See, but the only thing is with the P-51, I was already -- I mean -- I only saw the P-51 maybe two or three missions. The rest of the time I flew with P-38s and P-48s, you know. Another thing is -- I didn't mention this one here -- when the P-51s first come out, they looked like an ME-109. They looked a lot like the ME-109. In fact, I think they copied the ME-109 to build the 51. Now, he could -- they could go with us, see, because they carried tanks and dropped tanks and stuff like that there. But the P-51, what was happening is American soldiers were shooting down these P-51s because they looked so much like an ME-109. So what happened is there was a colonel gonna come over and do aerial acrobatics and show us what this P-51 looked like in the air, you know. So he's up there, you know, coming across the field. He did a couple -- a couple low flights over the field and went up in the air and in different ways and everything. And then it was kind of like over with, you know. And I was standing on the wing of our V-24. I was standing on the wing and I was watching him, you know. I mean here he comes man. He's really rolling. Man, he's coming down there like that there. I mean I know he wasn't near me. I mean he wasn't near me, but I still dropped down on the wing because I thought he was, you know. He come right over the top of me. And it looked to me like he was trying to get out or something, you know, like he was trying to get out of the plane. Well, he hit this hangar. The hangar had nothing by girders. It was just steel, I mean no shell. I mean it didn't have any, you know, cover over it. It just had these steel girders, you know, that make up this hangar. He hit that God damn hangar, and there was no fire or nothing because he just ground that plane up to nothing. I think the biggest thing they found was about half of one of these bones here man. He hit the -- I don't know what the hell happened to him, but boy he hit that hangar and, wow, that was the end of him. Evidently, something failed or he must have misjudged that ground. A lot of times when planes are flying they will misjudge the ground, you know, how close the ground is to them. Evidently, he either did that or something in the plane failed, but boy he hit that God damn -- he hit that -- he hit that hangar and hit them steel girders. They found him over, I think, down about a half mile -- about a half mile from where he hit it, you know, all tore up. He just ground that plane up into nothing. There was no airplane. It was just pieces of stuff sitting around, you know. Let's see. When we first got there we used to -- we used to share this base with -- we used to share this base with British -- they called them night fighters. They would fly at night only. One night we were out there. This is when we first got there. I don't know if we had flown a mission yet or not. But, anyhow, one of them had crashed on take-off or something happened, and a couple guys got burnt up and bullets were flying all over the place, you know, from the fire. And, you know, that kind of shook us up, you know, with that -- with that thing happening before we even started to fly, you know. Like I said, I'm not sure what happened to that plane, but he -- he burned right on the runway. I mean if he blew a tire or what the hell he did, you know, to crash right on the runway. He was just taking off, too. And then bombs -- the bombs were going off. But the ammunition was flying all over the place, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Get any mail or parcels while you were in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. Uh-hum. I got mail. I got mail from home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. Most of it was censored. I didn't get much -- I didn't get much. I think I got one or two letters but I got letters that -- in fact, see, I have six children. A lot of my stuff they have. But I have a book -- let's see if I could find it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So, let's see. When does it stop? When was your last mission?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: May 24th.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Okay. You even wrote -- that's what you finish this off with, the stuff you wrote about the prison camp, too.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. I might have. It might be in there. I'm not sure what's in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: There's an entry from April 29th, 1945.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Well, that's when I was liberated. That's the day I was liberated. Uh-hum. See, but most of that stuff at the prison camp was all written on cigarette wrappers.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And you just put it in later.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So January 1st looks like is where it starts in Italy.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Right. That's just about when we start. I think our first mission was early January.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Your first mission. It looks like you had a couple of attempts to fly your first mission.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Yeah. Call back. They called us back because _____+.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So maybe -- it looks like possibly, Cancels my second mission. So your first and second mission were canceled because of problems.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Might have been.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Looks like January 10th of '44 might be when you actually --

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Does it say _____?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I closed it up.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: January 7th. You said the 10th.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: All I got is railroad yard, Yugoslavia. See, I flew with another crew, Forbes (ph) crew.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you think we've covered it?

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: I think we've covered it pretty good. I mean you think you --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I mean you covered -- I didn't have to ask you questions because you were covering that territory.

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Uh-hum. Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Exactly. Oh, yeah, as far as Red Cross parcels, I usually ask about that, but you probably got the usual --

sp.speaker: Albert J. Yano
sp.p: Half a package or quarter package, yes. I got a package from home. I think I got pancake flower and a pair of socks. Everything else was gone.
